assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Kiyotaki-Moore mechanism, in which collateral values and credit constraints amplify and propagate shocks, is a foundational idea in macro-finance. It underpins much modern work on financial frictions, crises and policy. Its influence reaches theory, quantitative macro and policy analysis, and it is one of the clearest conceptual contributions on the list.
assessment.attribution: Kiyotaki and Moore (JPE 1997) is the core contribution, so the proposed credit goes to the two of them. The financial accelerator is a related but distinct strand of work by Bernanke, Gertler and Gilchrist. Bernanke already received the 2022 prize, which complicates adding Gertler or Gilchrist.
assessment.maturity: Nearly three decades of confirmation, with extensive empirical, quantitative and policy follow-up, notably after the 2008 crisis. Timing is not a concern.
uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers to pair this with the financial accelerator literature, which would change the laureate set.
Overlap with the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises (Bernanke, Diamond, Dybvig).

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The task-based view of technology and labour demand, together with the China-shock evidence on local labour-market adjustment, has changed how economists and policymakers think about inequality, automation and trade. The work combines conceptual framing with credible, widely replicated empirical designs.
assessment.attribution: Autor features across both the task framework and the trade-shock work, Hanson and Dorn are central to the trade-shock papers, and Katz is a major earlier co-contributor on skill-biased change. The three-name cap forces a hard choice, and the task-model theory also draws on Acemoglu and Restrepo, who are not credited here.
assessment.maturity: The work is roughly 10 to 20 years old and has been tested extensively. Some interpretations of the China shock remain debated, but the core empirical findings are well established.
uncertainties: Katz is omitted because of the three-laureate limit, which creates an attribution risk.
Debate over the long-run persistence and interpretation of the trade-shock effects.
Overlap with the 2024 prize on institutions and the 2019 prize on development experiments is limited.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: HANK models integrate household heterogeneity and the distribution of wealth and marginal propensities to consume into monetary and fiscal transmission. They are among the most significant methodological shifts in macroeconomics in the past decade and are now standard in central-bank and academic work. The central insight is that transmission operates largely through indirect general-equilibrium effects.
assessment.attribution: Kaplan, Moll and Violante (AER 2018) is the clear anchor and the three-name set is natural. The broader heterogeneous-agent tradition draws on Aiyagari, Bewley, Huggett and Krusell-Smith, so credit is a little diffuse, but the HANK synthesis is distinctly theirs.
assessment.maturity: Relatively recent, with the core paper from 2018. Adoption has been fast, but the long-run empirical verdict on how much HANK changes policy conclusions is still developing, so it may be somewhat early.
uncertainties: Timing: the framework may be early for a prize.
Whether the committee sees HANK as a culmination or as one stage in a broader heterogeneous-agent tradition.
Related macro work by committee colleagues could raise perceived conflicts of interest.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population-scale administrative data has transformed the measurement of intergenerational mobility, neighbourhood effects and the geography of opportunity. The work combines new measurement with quasi-experimental designs and has had strong policy impact. The conceptual contribution is smaller than the data and empirical contribution.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is clearly central across the program. Hendren, Friedman and Katz are core co-authors on specific papers, notably the mobility atlas and the Moving to Opportunity reanalysis. The three-name limit makes the credit allocation uncertain, and Chetty's contributions also appear in the public-economics candidate B027.
assessment.maturity: The main results come from the 2014-2022 period. They have been replicated and extended, but the time horizon is short for a prize and some causal interpretations are still debated.
uncertainties: Maturity: much of the work is recent.
Overlap of Chetty with the optimal-taxation candidate, and the wide range of his work.
Whether the committee values measurement and data innovation as much as a conceptual advance.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The BLP demand-estimation framework and the dynamic industry models (Ericson-Pakes, Olley-Pakes) are the standard toolkit for empirical industrial organisation and merger analysis. They are used across antitrust practice, trade and productivity measurement. The methodological and applied reach is very broad.
assessment.attribution: Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes (1995) is the core contribution, with Pakes also central to the dynamic and productivity-estimation strands. Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin are significant, but the three-name limit leaves some of them out.
assessment.maturity: Three decades of use and refinement. Highly confirmed in practice, with some ongoing debate about identification and the robustness of structural assumptions.
uncertainties: Attribution is spread over a large group of IO contributors.
Whether the committee prefers structural methodology over more conceptual advances.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Heterogeneous-firm trade models changed how economists think about who trades, selection into exporting, and the aggregate gains from trade, linking trade to firm-level productivity. The framework spawned a large empirical and quantitative literature and shaped policy analysis.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (Econometrica 2003) is the pivotal paper. Helpman has a broad foundational record in trade, including Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple on exporting versus FDI. Redding's contribution to the quantitative and spatial extensions is substantial but later. Bernard, Eaton and Kortum, who are not credited here, also contributed to the firm-level evidence and theory.
assessment.maturity: More than twenty years of confirmation, with abundant firm-level evidence. Krugman's 2008 prize partly covers new trade theory, which may crowd the topic.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2008 prize.
Omission of other firm-level trade contributors from the credited set.
Some debate about how much the aggregate gains from trade depend on the firm-heterogeneity channel.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Resource-misallocation accounting reframed the sources of cross-country income differences, showing how frictions that distort the allocation of inputs across firms can have large aggregate productivity effects. It links micro data to development and growth, and has been extremely influential in both fields. The mapping from measured dispersion to true distortions depends on strong assumptions, so the results are partly model-dependent.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh-Klenow (QJE 2009) and Restuccia-Rogerson (2008) are the anchors. Rogerson is not in the credited names, so the set is incomplete, and agricultural-productivity work by Restuccia and co-authors is a related strand. Disclosure: I have a long-standing collaboration with Peter Klenow, and this should be weighed in reading my ranking.
assessment.maturity: More than fifteen years of use, with active debate about measurement error and what dispersion in marginal products really identifies. Confirmation is strong in influence and moderate in identification.
uncertainties: Conflict: co-authorship with Klenow, which I disclose but which is not adjudicated.
Measurement-error critiques of dispersion-based misallocation measures.
Rogerson's absence from the credited names leaves attribution incomplete.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The alternating-offers bargaining model gave non-cooperative game theory a tractable and widely used account of negotiation. It links bargaining to patience and outside options, and was extended to decentralized markets through search-based bargaining. Its influence runs through labour, monetary and political-economy models, and it is a lasting theoretical contribution.
assessment.attribution: Rubinstein (Econometrica 1982) is the central contribution. Rubinstein-Wolinsky on markets with bargaining is the main extension. Binmore's role in the related bargaining literature (including with Rubinstein and Wolinsky on the Nash program and the outside-option principle) is real but less central to the originating result, and Stahl's earlier finite-horizon work is a precursor.
assessment.maturity: More than forty years old, so the contribution is very well established. The main concern is the passage of time relative to other areas, since game theory has been well recognised in earlier prizes.
uncertainties: Whether the committee judges bargaining theory to be adequately covered by earlier game-theory and mechanism-design prizes.
Credit split between Rubinstein and Binmore.
